description: High school seniors seeking an interactive way to share the history of space with curious minds interested in science
summary:
Night Shift at NASA is an educational video game that combines mystery, adventure, and science to bring NASA’s forgotten space equipment and missions to life.

The game follows Jassmin, a janitor working the night shift at an old NASA storage facility, where he encounters mysterious ghosts connected to past space missions. As players explore the building, solve puzzles, and investigate clues, they uncover the stories behind equipment left on the Moon, such as the Lunar Roving Vehicle and the Apollo Lunar Module descent stages.

Rather than simply presenting scientific facts, the game encourages players to discover these stories for themselves by asking questions, examining evidence, and thinking critically. Our goal is to show that these machines are more than abandoned equipment: they are an important part of human history whose stories deserve to be remembered and shared with new generations.
details:
One of the main ideas behind Night Shift at NASA was to make learning about space exploration feel like an adventure rather than a traditional lesson. We wanted players to become curious about the objects they encounter and discover the science behind them through exploration and problem-solving.

Throughout the game, players can explore different rooms, interact with objects, collect clues, and solve puzzles connected to real NASA missions. Each area introduces new information about the equipment and its historical importance. We focused on objects such as the Lunar Roving Vehicle and the Apollo Lunar Module descent stages, using their real functions and contributions to space exploration as the foundation for the game's challenges.

An important feature of our project is the way it approaches information and critical thinking. The ghosts are not always reliable sources, so players must question what they hear, investigate their surroundings, compare clues with verified information, and decide what to believe. This mechanic encourages players to think independently instead of accepting everything they are told.

To make the experience more engaging, we incorporated fictional characters, supernatural elements, humor, puzzles, and multiple possible endings. Although the story includes fictional events, the scientific and historical information is based on research from official NASA sources. This allowed us to combine creative storytelling with educational accuracy.

For development, we used Cursor to assist with coding, GitHub to manage and organize our work, Supabase for the project's backend services, and Vercel to deploy the game online. We also used artificial intelligence as a tool to help create some of the characters and visual elements.

We designed the game primarily for teenagers aged 13 and older, while keeping it accessible and enjoyable for anyone interested in science and space exploration. We wanted the challenges to encourage curiosity and problem-solving without requiring players to have previous knowledge of astronomy or engineering.

What makes Night Shift at NASA different is its approach to science communication. Instead of separating education from entertainment, we integrated scientific discoveries into the gameplay itself. Every object, clue, and puzzle serves as an opportunity to learn something about the history of space exploration.

Ultimately, we hope this project inspires younger generations to look beyond the surface of scientific discoveries, ask questions, and develop a greater appreciation for the people, technology, and missions that have helped humanity explore the universe. Even equipment that has been left behind can still have a story worth discovering.
